analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 30% minimum tax rate on incomes above $1 million.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 10 cosponsors in April 2017 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require taxpayers with adjusted gross incomes over $1 million to pay at least 30% of that income in federal taxes, after allowing for charitable deductions. It would count income tax, the alternative minimum tax, and payroll taxes toward that minimum, phase in just above the $1 million threshold, and adjust the threshold for inflation after 2018. The bill's stated purpose is to reduce the deficit by billions of dollars a year and ensure the highest earners pay a minimum effective rate.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly: the Congressional Budget Office has long estimated that a Buffett-rule-style minimum tax on millionaires raises tens of billions of dollars a year, money that can reduce deficits or offset other tax increases. Middle- and lower-income taxpayers pay nothing under the bill — the threshold is $1 million in annual income. It also reduces the advantage very high earners currently get from preferential rates and deductions that lower their effective tax rates below what middle-income wage earners pay.

how_it_helps.text: Applies only to taxpayers with adjusted gross income over $1 million, leaving 99%+ of taxpayers untouched.
Guarantees a 30% minimum effective rate on income above that threshold, after a charitable-deduction offset, closing the gap between what millionaires and ordinary wage earners pay.
Counts regular income tax, the alternative minimum tax, and payroll taxes toward the minimum, and phases the tax in above $1 million so it is not a cliff.
The bill states its purpose as cutting the deficit by billions of dollars a year and serving as a floor on taxes for the highest-income taxpayers.
Adjusts the $1 million threshold for inflation after 2018 so the tax does not gradually reach down into middle incomes.

analysis.who_pays: Households with more than $1 million in annual adjusted gross income — roughly the top fraction of one percent of filers — would pay tens of thousands of dollars or more per year in additional federal tax. Estates, trusts, and very high earners who currently lower their effective rates through itemized deductions would see the largest increases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households earning over $1 million a year

drawbacks.text: The bill raises revenue through a parallel minimum-tax structure layered on top of the existing income tax, the AMT, and payroll taxes — adding complexity to a tax code that the bill itself says should be simplified.

The charitable-deduction carve-out lets high-income taxpayers who give heavily reduce the base on which the 30% minimum applies, a concession that shrinks revenue and adds a special rule critics could call a loophole.

A minimum tax on millionaires raises a comparatively small share of federal revenue; by itself it does not close long-term budget gaps, which the bill acknowledges by calling itself an 'interim step' toward broader tax reform.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is favorable to the vast majority of taxpayers: no one under $1 million in income pays anything, and the added revenue modestly reduces deficits. The main costs fall on a very small group of very high earners. The bill's weaknesses are design, not distribution — it stacks a new minimum tax on an already complex code and carves out charitable deductions, which is why it presents itself as an interim step rather than full reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the Paying a Fair Share Act of 2017 on April 26, 2017, joined by seven original cosponsors including Reps. Delaney, Lee, Langevin, Pocan, Schakowsky, Slaughter, and Clark.
Ten Democratic House members cosponsored the bill in total; no Republican signed on.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on April 26, 2017, and that was its last action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred.
The bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without ever advancing past its committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning over $1 million a year are better off, since they avoided a 30% minimum tax rate that would have added tens of thousands of dollars to their annual bills. The Ways and Means Committee's decision to never act on the bill preserved the status quo for high earners.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income households, whose taxes stayed as they were

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 26, 2017, framing it as a deficit-reduction measure imposing a minimum tax rate on millionaires.

for.name: 10 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Delaney, Lee, Langevin, Pocan, Schakowsky, Slaughter, and Clark.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 26, 2017 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor calendar and committee agendas in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor or scheduled committee action on it, while the majority pursued its own tax overhaul (the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act) in late 2017 that instead lowered rates for high earners and corporations.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and the bill sat in committee under a Republican majority for the entire 115th Congress; no Republican supported it.

industries.industry: Households earning over $1 million a year
industries.note: The top fraction of one percent of filers would owe tens of thousands of dollars more per year, since the bill guarantees a 30% effective rate after charitable deductions. Their interest in blocking it ran against the bill's stated goal of deficit reduction paid for by high earners.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax planning industry
industries.note: A new parallel minimum tax adds computations that high-income clients would need professional help with, but the bill never became law, so the industry gained nothing. Wealthy filers' continued use of complex deductions and preferential rates — which this bill would have overridden — supports demand for planning services.
